questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Reason for a Discontinuity
questions.problem:
For what reason does the function $f(x)$ given below have a discontinuity at $x=2?$

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}, & x<2 \\ 4, & x=2 \\ -2x, & x>2\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2.$

- $f(2)=4,$ so $f(2)$ exists. $✓$

- We calculate the one-sided limits and check if they coincide:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}(-{x}^{2}) \\  & =-{2}^{2} \\  & =-4, \\ {lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}(-2x) \\  & =-2\cdot 2 \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the overall limit exists and ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)=-4$ $✓$

- The limit of the function is not equal to the function value: ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)=-4,$ while $f(2)=4.$ $\,\,\times $

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=2$ because ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)\ne f(2).$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Reason for a Discontinuity
questions.problem:
For what reason does the function $f(x)$ given below have a discontinuity at $x=3?$

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{x-3}, & x<3 \\ -\frac{5}{x-3}, & x>3\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=3.$

- We have that $f(3)$ is not defined since $x=3$ does not belong to the domain of $f(x).$ $\times $

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=3$ because $f(3)$ does not exist.

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Definition of Continuity to Evaluate a Limit
questions.problem:
If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-\frac{3}{5}$ and ${lim}_{x\to {(-3/5)}^{-}}f(x)=7,$ then

$f(-\frac{3}{5})=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-\frac{3}{5}.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that ${lim}_{x\to (-3/5)}f(x)$ exists, and

$$
f(-\frac{3}{5})={lim}_{x\to (-3/5)}f(x)={lim}_{x\to {(-3/5)}^{-}}f(x)=7.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Definition of Continuity to Evaluate a Limit
questions.problem:
If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=3$ and $f(3)=-3,$ then

${lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}\frac{x+(f(x))^{3}}{2}=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=3.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that ${lim}_{x\to 3}f(x)$ exists and

$$
{lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to 3}f(x)=f(3)=-3.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}\frac{x+(f(x))^{3}}{2} & =\frac{3+(-3)^{3}}{2}=-12.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Definition of Continuity to Evaluate a Limit
questions.problem:
If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-2$ and $f(-2)=2,$ then

${lim}_{x\to -{2}^{-}}({x}^{3}+2(f(x))^{2})=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-2.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that ${lim}_{x\to -2}f(x)$ exists and

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{2}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to -2}f(x)=f(-2)=2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{2}^{-}}({x}^{3}+2(f(x))^{2}) & =(-2)^{3}+2(-2)^{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$
